title: The C switch bug that compiles clean: missing break
description:
In C, forgetting a break inside a switch doesn't cause an error. Execution falls through into the next case and quietly runs code you never asked for. Here's how fall-through works, why one matched case can print two lines, and the one time you actually want it.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/c-mastery-path/level-1/03-control-flow/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Here's a C bug that compiles clean and still burns you. You write a switch, one case matches, and somehow two lines print. No warning, no error.
The value is one, so the first case runs. But there's no break after it, so execution just keeps going, straight down into case two. That's fall-through.
It's not always a bug. Stacked cases with no break let A, B, and C share one handler. When you do that on purpose, leave a fallthrough comment so the next reader knows.
So the rule: every case ends with break, unless you meant to fall through and said so. Miss one, and the compiler stays quiet.
